central_question: Why does a coffee mug stay hot even after the liquid is gone?
hook: You finish your last sip, the mug is empty, yet it still feels warm to the touch. How can a cup that’s lost its coffee still keep heat?
aha_moment: The ceramic wall itself becomes a hot reservoir: its high heat capacity stores energy, and its low thermal conductivity plus an insulating air cavity slow the loss of that heat.

story_arc.reveal: The mug stays warm after the coffee is gone.

story_arc.purpose: Opening promise – hint at a concrete answer
story_arc.reveal: We’ll uncover why the ceramic wall keeps the heat.
required_facts: ceramic wall has high heat capacity

story_arc.reveal: During brewing, ~200 g of coffee pours 130 kJ into the ~150 g ceramic wall.
Even after the liquid leaves, the wall still holds ~130 kJ of heat.

story_arc.purpose: Second reveal – how heat can leave
story_arc.reveal: Heat exits only by conduction through ceramic, convection to room air, and radiation.
While coffee was present, evaporation removed ~80 % of heat; once gone, that fast loss channel disappears.

story_arc.purpose: Third reveal – slow cooling after evaporation
story_arc.reveal: With evaporation gone, the wall cools only a few kelvin per minute via weak convection and radiation.
A metal mug, with high conductivity, spreads heat quickly and feels cooler after the coffee is poured out.
That lingering warmth is why ceramic mugs are preferred for hot drinks and even in space where heat retention matters.

ending_payoff: So the next time you touch an empty mug and feel a gentle heat, remember it’s the ceramic wall’s stubborn, slow‑cooling reservoir doing the work—proof that even ordinary objects have a hidden physics story.
